lead: Every IoT device is three buyable parts around its sensors: a control unit that computes, a communication module that carries bits, and a power source that feeds both. Choose one badly and the others suffer: a fast radio empties a coin cell in hours; a slow processor cannot encrypt in time. This chapter names each part and its options, then gives a selection procedure.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for the five-block picture of a sensor node.

sections.h3: Control unit: the part that computes

blocks.text: The control unit runs the program, reads sensors and decides what to send. A microcontroller (MCU) puts CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals on one chip and runs bare-metal code or a small real-time OS, not Linux. An applications processor or system-on-chip (SoC) runs Linux and draws far more current. Chapter 2.5 compares them at board level; here you only size one.
A node reading a sensor once a minute and sending 20 bytes needs about 32–64 kB flash, 8 kB RAM and a 16 MHz clock. More is paid for in current every second.
The blocks built around the CPU:

items: Clock: crystal or internal oscillator sets instruction speed and wake accuracy.
Memory: flash holds code across power cuts, SRAM variables, EEPROM or FRAM calibration.
GPIO: general-purpose input/output pins read or drive one logic level, 0 V or 3.3 V.
ADC: analog-to-digital converter turns a voltage into a number, 10 or 12 bits against a reference.
PWM: pulse-width modulation, a square wave whose duty cycle sets average voltage; used for dimming and motor speed.
Timers: counters that trigger a sample or wake the chip at a fixed interval.

blocks.text: Three serial buses link CPU to outside. UART: two wires, one device per port, e.g. 9600 baud to GPS. SPI: four wires, fastest, for flash and displays. I²C: two wires shared by up to 127 addressed devices, usual for sensors.

sections.h3: Communication module: the part that talks

blocks.text: A radio is a chain, not a chip. The transceiver generates and detects the modulated signal. A matching network of inductors and capacitors transforms its impedance to 50 Ω. The antenna radiates. A matching error costs range and can push emissions past the legal limit.

Most products use a pre-certified module: transceiver, matching network, antenna and shield in one metal can, approved for sale, with protocol firmware (the stack) inside. A bare chip plus your own antenna means months of testing.
These are typical, not guaranteed. Indoor range is often a third of open-air, and a concrete wall costs several dB. Protocol detail belongs to Unit 3.

sections.h3: Power source: the part that pays

items: Mains adaptor: unlimited energy, but a wire and fixed position.
Primary cell: alkaline or lithium AA/AAA, or coin cell such as CR2032 at roughly 220 mAh; not rechargeable.
Rechargeable Li-ion or LiPo: 3.7 V nominal, high current, needs protection.
Energy harvesting: solar, piezoelectric strip for vibration, thermoelectric generator for heat; tiny and intermittent.

blocks.text: Between cell and chip sits a regulator. An LDO (low-dropout linear regulator) is cheap and quiet but burns voltage drop as heat, so efficiency is roughly Vout ÷ Vin. A switching regulator (buck or boost) reaches 80–95% and adds switching noise. Check quiescent current (the regulator's own no-load draw). A 5 µA quiescent current against a 10 µA sleep load raises the sleep drain to 15 µA and cuts battery life to two-thirds; sleep life scales as I_sleep ÷ (I_sleep + I_q), where I_sleep is the sleep load and I_q is quiescent current. Halving needs I_q equal to the sleep load. Add undervoltage cutoff, reverse-polarity protection and a fuse, plus a fuel gauge (coulomb counter or voltage lookup) if the user must see charge.

blocks.where: t is battery life in hours; V_bat is cell voltage in V; Q_bat is cell capacity in Ah; η is regulator efficiency as a fraction; V_rail is the regulated supply in V; I_avg is the average current drawn by the load in A.

sections.h3: Optional blocks and a selection procedure

blocks.text: A security element stores keys and runs AES or elliptic-curve signing in hardware, so a stolen node cannot be cloned and its key never leaves the chip. A real-time clock (RTC) is a 32.768 kHz crystal and counter, often coin-cell backed, that keeps wall-clock time and wakes the control unit.
Selection runs in one direction, because each choice constrains the next:

items: Fix application: what is measured, how often, and how far data travels.
Set required range and data rate; pick radio from table.
Compute energy per day: sum V × I × t over active, radio-on and sleep time.
Divide cell energy by daily energy for life in days; if it fails, cut duty cycle before changing cell.
Pick control unit: enough ADC channels, buses, flash for crypto stack, solderable package.
Check peak: a Wi-Fi burst of about 300 mA cannot come from a CR2032; add a supercapacitor or choose a smaller radio.

examples.question: A node runs from a 3.7 V, 1200 mAh Li-ion cell. The 3.3 V rail draws 30 mA on average; the regulator is 85% efficient. Find battery life. What is the life if sleep scheduling lowers the average to 3 mA?
steps: Check ratio: current fell ten times and life rose ten times, because life is inversely proportional to average current (t ∝ 1 ÷ I_avg).
examples.answer: About 38.1 h at 30 mA, rising to 381.2 h ≈ 15.9 days at 3 mA.
examples.check:
V_bat = 3.7
Q_bat = 1.2
eta = 0.85
E = V_bat * Q_bat
print(round(E, 2))
for I in (0.030, 0.003):
    P_in = 3.3 * I / eta
    print(round(E / P_in, 2))
t_sleep = E / (3.3 * 0.003 / eta)
print(round(t_sleep / 24, 2))

traps: Sizing a battery from mAh alone: mAh is charge, mA is current, and regulator efficiency sits between them. Convert to Wh and W first.
Picking a radio by data rate only. A 100 Mbps Wi-Fi link on a coin cell lasts hours; a 250 kbps ZigBee link lasts months.
Forgetting regulator quiescent current at microamp sleep: 5 µA against a 10 µA sleep load cuts sleep life to two-thirds; doubling needs I_q equal to the sleep load.
Assuming a small cell can deliver any peak current. The radio's transmit burst, not the average, decides brownout.
Quoting open-air range as real range; walls and interference cut it, and examiners ask why.

quiz.q: Name the three parts beside the sensors and one example of each.
quiz.a: Control unit (microcontroller), communication module (Wi-Fi or BLE module), power source (Li-ion or coin cell).

quiz.q: Why does an LDO waste more power as input voltage rises above output?
quiz.a: It drops the difference as heat at full load current; loss is (Vin − Vout) × I. Efficiency ≈ Vout ÷ Vin falls as Vin rises.

quiz.q: A node draws 20 mA at 3.3 V from a 3.7 V, 2000 mAh cell through a 90% efficient regulator. Find life in hours.
A CR2032 holds about 220 mAh. A BLE beacon averages 3 µA sleep current. What sleep life does the cell alone give, in years?
A field soil-moisture node is specified with Wi-Fi. Which two parts conflict, and what change?
quiz.a: Radio and power source. Wi-Fi's 300 mA bursts and short range suit mains power; a battery drains and may brown out. Move to LoRa or NB-IoT for kilometres at low rate, cut duty cycle, keep MCU asleep between samples.

quiz.q: Why does a pre-certified radio module shorten a product schedule?
quiz.a: Transceiver, matching network, antenna and approvals are done, and the protocol stack ships with it, so you skip RF layout, matching and certification testing.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the control unit and radio are often one part: chips such as ESP32 or nRF52 combine an MCU core, flash and a 2.4 GHz radio on one die, which is why hobby boards are cheap. Dedicated harvesting ICs cold-start from a few hundred millivolts of solar or thermoelectric input. Research goes into battery-free and intermittent computing, where a node loses power mid-task and must resume safely. Search terms: system-on-chip IoT, RF matching network, quiescent current, energy harvesting PMIC, Thread and Matter.
